CausalChain: Chronic liver inflammation/HBV/HCV infection -> Elevated IL-6 secretion from tumor and stromal cells -> IL-6 binds to IL-6R, activating JAK and STAT3 -> Overactivated STAT3 increases transcription of anti-apoptotic genes, cancer stem cell markers, angiogenic factors, and PD-L1 -> Downregulation or epigenetic silencing of SOCS proteins removes negative feedback on STAT3 -> Sustained STAT3 signaling promotes tumor progression and immune escape -> Restoring SOCS function or simulating its inhibitory effect reduces STAT3 activation, leading to decreased PD-L1 expression and sensitization to chemotherapy
Hypothesis: Restoration or pharmacological mimicry of SOCS activity in HCC will inhibit IL-6/STAT3 driven tumor cell survival, cancer stem cell maintenance, and immune evasion. Specifically, combining SOCS-restorative strategies with STAT3 inhibitors will reduce PD-L1 expression and enhance the therapeutic efficacy of conventional treatments against HCC.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is often driven by chronic inflammatory signals, particularly those emerging from persistent interleukin‐6 (IL-6) secretion that activates the signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) pathway. Recent studies have implicated continuous STAT3 activation in promoting cancer stem cell enrichment, resistance to apoptosis, induction of angiogenesis, and immune escape via PD-L1 upregulation. Notably, the negative-feedback regulators including suppressors of cytokine signaling (SOCS) proteins, which normally temper this pathway, are frequently downregulated in HCC. In this context, we propose that restoring SOCS activity or mimicking its effects may synergize with direct STAT3 inhibition to attenuate tumor progression and overcome immune evasion. Together, these interventions could not only downregulate PD-L1 expression but also sensitize HCC cells to chemotherapeutic agents, thus providing a novel therapeutic approach in the management of HCC.
